newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese minister says army may impose curfew.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese minister says army may impose curfew.

text.p: Lebanon's interior minister said on Wednesday the army had the authority to impose a curfew to prevent opposition demonstrations on Thursday but stopped short of saying it would do so.

Michel al-Murr, who is also deputy prime minister, said street protests planned for Beirut and other cities during a general strike were banned and it was up to the army and security forces to maintain security.

The last time the opposition called a general strike and street protests, on February 29, the army slapped a curfew on most of the country for much of the day and arrested thousands of curfew breakers.
Opposition groups and labour unions have called Thursday's strike and demonstrations to protest against the media and social policies of the government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.
Questioned by reporters in parliament during a confidence debate on Hariri's new government, Murr appeared to indicate the likelihood that troops might be used again.
"There is a previous decision taken by the government banning demonstrations and this decision is still valid today," he said.
"The task of the army and security forces is to maintain security in the country and they take the measures needed for this task," he added.
Asked whether the army might impose a curfew, Murr said: "This is not our responsibility....If the army found that the situation needed a curfew declaration, it could do so."
Hariri has imposed a ban on all demonstrations since 1993.
Cancellation of the ban is one of three main demands of a broad spectrum of political parties, unions, students and media workers who issued the strike and demonstration call last week.

They are also protesting against the government's perceived failure to improve social conditions for the vast majority of Lebanese, many of whom live below the poverty line, and against a decision to close scores of radio and television stations on Saturday.
The opposition says the way the government is applying a new law regulating the audiovisiual media will muzzle the opposition and carve up the lucrative media market among its friends.

Only a handful of broadcasting licences have been granted, mostly to establishment figures like Hariri, and all opposition stations are to close. The move will reduce the number of broadcasters to 15 from about 150 and put some 2,000 media workers out of a job.

The pro-Iranian Hizbollah (Party of God) threw its weight behind the planned protests on Tuesday, raising the prospect that thousands of its Shi'ite Moslem supporters might try to take to the streets in Beirut and other cities.

"Let it (the strike) be a resounding cry in the face of those responsible so they may wake up from their slumber and begin to understand the extent of the suffering around them," Hizbollah said in a statement.
